message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few key factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects the sky, so it can look light‑blue or even greenish. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange) and scatters shorter ones (blue, green), giving a deeper blue or indigo hue. |
| **Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water lets you see the seabed and any underlying colors (sand, rocks, algae). Turbid or muddy water scatters light more, often producing a greenish or brownish tint. |
| **Algae & Phytoplankton** | High concentrations of green algae give the water a green or teal appearance. Certain phytoplankton blooms can even make the sea look reddish or orange. |
| **Sunlight Angle** | At sunrise or sunset, the light passes through more atmosphere, scattering reds and oranges, so the sea can take on warm hues. |
| **Atmospheric Conditions** | Overcast skies or haze can mute the blue, making the sea look gray or muted. |
| **Human Perception** | Our eyes and brains interpret the mix of reflected sky, scattered light, and surface features, so the same water can look slightly different to different observers. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” it can range from pale turquoise in shallow tropical waters to deep indigo in the open ocean, and even green, gray, or reddish under certain conditions.
